This event was preceded by a presidential order that reversed a transfer of authority in the Daniels bill, and the role of one man involved in it would lead to the investigation of money given by the Thomson-Urrutia Treaty. Another man associated with it was earlier involved in the inquiry into the Ballinger-Pinchot affair. One man associated with it avoided jail time but resigned as Secretary of the Navy, Edwin Denby. Name this event that stemmed from Edward Doheny and Harry Sinclair being granted rights to naval reserve lands by Interior Secretary Albert Fall, a scandal named for a Wyoming oil reserve, during the Harding administration.

This man was promoted to brevet major after the same battle that saw Santa Anna ride off and abandon his false leg; he received that promotion for finding a trail that allowed Winfield Scott's forces to flank and thus win the Battle of Cerro Gordo. Between those two posts, he assumed his most famous role by replacing Joseph Johnston and later won the Seven Days Battles, but only after spending a year serving as a senior military advisor to Jefferson Davis. Name this son of "Light Horse Harry" who was a top graduate of West Point and went on to lead the Army of Northern Virginia for the Confederacy during the Civil War.

The Anaconda Mining Company was founded in this state by Marcus Daly after a discovery of silver and copper deposits, and its town of Glasgow is located near its Fort Peck Lake. The Pompey's Pillar national monument in this state is notable for the signature of William Clark inscribed upon it. It has the distinction of being the only state with rivers that eventually flow into the Pacific Ocean, Gulf of Mexico, and Hudson Bay. Also home to the Glacier National park, the Clark, the Blackfoot and the Bitterroot Rivers run through Missoula in this state. Identify this state, whose largest city is Billings.

One account of this battle tells of the daring attack of Aminias. The day before this battle a prophecy Euphrantides led to the sacrifice of three men related to the opposing commander; that commander watched this battle from Mount Aegaleos. Damasithymus was attacked by an ally, but this attack was mistaken by both sides as favorable and allowed for the escape of Artemisia. A few weeks prior to this engagement, Ephialtes' betrayal allowed the aggressor's forces to overcome the defense led by Leonidas at Thermopylae. Name this battle that saw Xerxes I's fleet defeated by Themistocles, named for an island near Athens.

The Basilica of Saint Martin was near the location of one battle fought here, an action that was followed up by the battle of the River Berre. That battle fought here occurred shortly after the battles of the River Garonne and Bordeaux at which Odo, the duke of Aquitaine, was routed. One winning side at this location was commanded by a man who served the Merovingians as mayor of the palace, while another victor at this site captured John II and was Edward, the Black Prince. Name this site where Abd ar-Rahman was hammered by Charles Martel, which, was the site of a 1356 British victory in the Hundred Years' War that is not Agincourt or Crecy.

This man ordered Richard Bayfield's burning at the stake, and also persecuted John Frith. This man led a campaign against collaborators of William Tyndale while in his highest post, in which he was replaced by Thomas Audley after his failure to attend a certain wedding and his refusal to sign the Act of Supremacy. This man translated the first Pico della Mirandola biography into English, and established a friendship with Erasmus during Erasmus's visit to his country. Name this patron saint of politicians and Lord Chancellor to Henry VIII, who got his head chopped off in 1535 and wrote Utopia.

Robert Remini argued in one of his works that Martin van Buren did not introduce this bill to congress just to have it defeated, and support for this bill grew after a meeting in Harrisburg. One writing against this bill declares that there is a "striking distinction between Government and Sovereignty," and that this bill supported the "protection of one branch of industry at the expense of others." Those words appeared in John Calhoun's South Carolina Exposition and Protest, and this bill raised the tax on several imported goods. Name this tariff that was signed into law by John Quincy Adams, with a repulsive nickname.

This man's mother lived too close to his father Senzangakona for him to be considered legitimate, and he was exiled after allowing a sheep to die. In one instance, he reportedly slaughtered forty oxen and 7000 people, including two girls who were buried alive with his mother, Nandi. He required his army to jog barefoot over thorny ground, introduced the weapons known as the iklwa and the assegai, a formation which involved the "chest," the "loins," and "horns" of the buffalo, and regiments with color-coded shields known as impi. Name this man largely responsible for the mfecane in southern Africa, the ruler of the Zulu.

This man attempted to formally legalize his leadership by passing the Organic Laws, one of which, the Law of Succession, declared the government a monarchy and gave him the power to name his successor. His deputy prime minister was assassinated in a car bombing two years before this man would himself die. One of his first major acts as head of state was the Decree of Unification, which merged all nationalist parties under his FET party. Prior to seizing power, this man had run afoul of the leftist Popular Front, which sent him to serve as the military commander of the Canary Islands. Undeterred, he helped spark an uprising which eventually led to the horrific bombing of the Basque town of Guernica. Identify this man, who was succeeded by King Juan Carlos I, the supreme leader of Spain from 1936 to 1975.

The majority opinion in this case compares the event at hand to that of the earlier Strauder v. West Virginia and refers to the precedent set by Roberts v. City of Boston. This opinion, written by Henry Billings Brown, rejected the arguments of counsel Albion Tourgée. This case's dissenting opinion contains the line "there is in this country no superior, dominant, ruling class of citizens," an idealistic statement that contrasts with the majority's opinion that legislation is "powerless to abolish distinctions based upon physical differences." name this 1896 U.S. Supreme Court case, in which John Marshall Harlan was the lone dissenter to a ruling that upheld "separate but equal" laws as constitutional.

The representative of Great Britain at the signing of this agreement was Lord Cushendun, while Count Manzoni represented Italy and William Lyon MacKenzie King represented Canada. Other countries who were signatories included Cuba and the "kingdom of the Serbs." One of its signatories had earlier won the Nobel Peace Prize for his work on the Locarno treaties. Ratified by the U.S. Senate on an 85 to 1 vote, this agreement was severely tested by the Mukden incident in Manchuria. The second of its namesake signatories would win the Peace Prize the year after this agreement's signing. Identify this 1928 agreement, named for the French Prime Minister and U.S. Secretary of State at the time, that boldly declared an outlawing of war.

This man labeled marriage as something that "must sooner or later come to pass," and had his teacher, the Earl of Bute, provide him with a list of eligible princesses before finally marrying Charlotte Sophia. Unable to form long-term alliances with such ministers as the Earl of Newcastle and George Grenville, he finally found a fruitful relationship with a man whom he would ultimately break with regarding the idea of Catholic emancipation to preserve unity with Ireland. Besides William Pitt the Younger, this man's ministers also included Lord North, who was forced out of office by a vote of no confidence after the battle of Yorktown. Identify this British monarch, noted for his violent mental breakdown late in his life and for reigning during the American Revolution.

Participants in this event included two former attorney generals, one of whom was Francis Biddle. Robert Ley was originally going to appear at this event, but killed himself about a month prior to its beginning. One of the men who helped conceive of this event was Murray Bernays, who came up with the idea to treat various groups as criminal organizations. While Sir Norman Birkett labeled it "a precedent of the highest standing," William O. Douglas argued that it was probably "unconstitutional by American standards." During this event, the oratory of Robert Jackson helped lead to the deaths of Alfred Rosenberg and Hans Frank. Hans Fritzche, Hjalmar Schacht, and Franz von Papen were the only three defendants acquitted at what series of trials, held to punish the leaders of Nazi Germany after World War II?

While none of this man's writings have survived, extant works include the speech he gave advocating the admission of Gauls into the Senate. He wrote a treatise on dice-playing and at least twenty tomes of Etruscan history. He helped reform the Roman judicial system, expanded the empire into Mauretania and Lycia, and avoided warring with the Germans. Seneca mocked him in a work titled for the Pumpkinification of this man. He began an invasion of Britain in C.E. 43, and made the mistake of marrying Agrippina, who was eager to advance her son's rise to power and probably ended up poisoning this man. Identify this Roman Emperor, who was succeeded by Nero, and is the narrator of a work of historical fiction by Robert Graves.

This man married a Native American woman named Morning Mist of the Haida tribe, who died five years after their marriage in 1856. During the so-called Pig War with Great Britain, he defended San Juan Island from British warships. One of this man's most grievous defeats occurred in April 1865 when he was enjoying a fish fry picnic with his officers and arrived too late to rally his troops against Union attack at Five Forks. Promoted to major general in 1862, some of his brigadier generals included Richard Garnett and Lewis Armistead, both of whom died in the battle this man is most associated with. Along with Johnston Pettigrew and Isaac Trimble, this man participated in an action that occurred after two hours of artillery barrage on Cemetery Ridge. Identify this Confederate general, best remembered for leading an ill-fated charge during the battle of Gettysburg.

This group's namesake bank began to decline when one of its members, nicknamed for his gout, refused to make loans to secular rulers. Benedetti Dei chronicled this group in The Report of the Years, and one member of this group was kept prisoner at the Castel Sant'Angelo during Colonna's sack of Rome and feuded with Henry VIII over the appointment of Thomas Cranmer. One member of this group excommunicated Martin Luther. In addition to Popes Clement VII and Leo X, one member of this group was killed in the Pazzi conspiracy. Name this Florentine family that included Cosimo and Lorenzo the Magnificent.

This man's death at Chimkent led to the division of his lands among all his male descendents, but that proved unstable and his empire was eventually re-united by his youngest son, Shah Rokh. His rise to power began when he left Amir Kazgan to enter the service of the Tughluq dynasty, then joined his brother-in-law Amir Husayn to conquer Transoxania. This ruler's forces suppressed the 1395 Persian revolt by constructing towers of skulls. The Gur-e Amir is the tomb of this ruler in the capital city where he shielded Tokhtamysh from the Russians, that city being Samarkand. Name this Islamic Turkic-Mongol conqueror epithetically known for his lame arm.

This group was granted special privelidges in Omni Datum Optimum, a bull of Innocent II. Founded by Hugh de Payns, this order was provided quarters by Baldwin II of Flanders, from the location of which quarters they derived their name. Members of this rival to the Hospitallers were purchased and executed en masse by Saladin after he won the Battle of Hattin. This order's last Grand Master, Hugh de Molay, burned at the stake at the behest of Phillip IV, who accused this order or heresy probably to sieze its assets. Name this original religious military order of Crusader knights founded to protect Christian pilgrims to Jerusalem.

This man's father died during Lord Dunmore's War, and he founded a settlement after hearing a vision from the Master of Life. This man's namesake conflict included a faction called the Red Sticks, and was spurred when a Lenape chief died, allegedly of witchcraft, and also stemmed from the Treaty of Fort Wayne. His alleged killer used a political slogan containing his name that began "Rumpsy Dumpsy." His brother was named Teskwatawa, and suffered defeat at the hands of William Henry Harrison at Tippecanoe. Name this brother of The Prophet, a Shawnee chief who was allegedly killed by Richard Mentor Johnson in the War of 1812.

One decree from this event mandated that sacred scripture and tradition be treated with equal "loyalty and reverence," while another calls for the "urgent fostering" of vocations. In addition to producing Dei Verbum and Optatam Totius, this event reaffirmed Providentissimus Deus and Divino Afflante Spiritu, and it was followed by a defense of clerical celibacy, Sacerdotalis Caelibatus. One text from this council absolved Jews of blood guilt, Nostra Aetate, while another discussed the place of the Church in the modern world, Gaudiem et Spes. Establishing the vernacular mass, name this Catholic ecumenical council convened by John XXIII in 1962.

One member of this group was a feeble Belgian-born farmer named Mr. Hardkoop who was turned away by the Kesebergs and allegedly sat on a log with his head in his hands. One of the financial backers of this group was Patrick Breen, and one leader of this group was James Reed. Their problems began when Lansford W. Hastings convinced them to take his namesake "cutoff," and a contingent of them known as the "Forlorn Hope" attempted to snowshoe to Sutter's Fort. Name this group that got stuck in the Sierra Nevadas on their way to California and resorted to cannibalism in their namesake pass.

In 1834, this man ran for governor of his home state on the Anti Masonic ticket but lost to John Davis. This president appointed Robert Trimble to the Supreme Court, and was ousted as incumbent in an election that saw his opponent's wife Rachel accused of bigamy. This defending attorney in the Amistad case sorted out border disputes and acquired Florida in a treaty signed with Spanish diplomat Luis Onis. He beat out William Crawford, among others, because no candidate won the majority of electoral votes in the election of 1824 that was swung by Henry Clay's "corrupt bargain." name this sixth president of the United States, son a president.

In Sheppard v. Maxwell, the Supreme Court ruled that this concept could not interfere with a defendant's right to trial. The case Near v. Minnesota stated that this concept would apply except only in rare cases, while a1971 case stated that restraints on this concept would only be allowed in "grave and irreparable danger." A 1964 case involving this concept involved a document called "Heed Their Rising Voices" and Alabama Police Commissioner L.B. Sullivan. Name this concept that was defended by Andrew Hamilton in the 1735 case of John Peter Zenger, which like Freedom of Speech is described in the First Amendment.

This man's daughter Maria wound up working as a circus tiger-trainer, and painted a saintly-looking picture of him included in her biography of this man, "My Father." This man was allegedly involved in an underground sect that allegedly practiced self-flagellation and held wild orgies, the Khlysty. He woke up Anya Vyrubova, who was in a coma after a train accident, and he was poisoned, shot three times, beaten with a dumbbell, and thrown in a river by conspirators led by Felix Yusupov. Name this Russian Holy man, the healer of Alexei Romanov and alleged sexual consort of the empress.

The most noted portrait of this man shows two stacks of three crowns above an ornate arch that surrounds his profile, and was painted by Gentile Bellini. This man's son sent his navy under Kemal Reis to bring the Jews and Arabs fleeing the Spanish Inquisition. A siege laid by this ruler caused Pope Callixtus III to excommunicate Halley's Comet. His expansion was checked by Skanderbeg's revolt, and was defeated in the Night Attack by Vlad Dracula. His greatest victory came over Constantine XI and resulted in the Hagia Sofia's conversion to a mosque. Succeeded by his son Bayezid II, name this sultan who sacked Constantinople in 1453.

Less notable aspects of this document include clauses that men can't be imprisoned because of a female claim unless it's in regards to the death of her husband, and that no town or person could be forced to build a bridge. This document also made it legal for Jews to practice usury, since they were not Christians, they could not be excommunicated for charging interest on loans. This document is perhaps more well known for the implementation of the concepts of habeas corpus and the establishment of a twenty-five baron council to keep the king in check. Name this document that greatly curtailed the power of King John, written in 1215.

This man once vetoed a bill to appropriate funds for drought-stricken Texas farmers by saying "federal aid…encourages the expectations of paternal care." He used the slogan "Public office is a public trust," and as President, had to deal with such incidents as a march on Washington led by Jacob Coxey. During this man's presidency, he also sent in the army to deal with a strike led by Eugene V. Debs, and this man signed both the Interstate Commerce Act and the Dawes Act. Identify this President who defeated both James G. Blaine and Benjamin Harrison to win two nonconsecutive terms.

Before the first battle at this location, poor communication involving the 10th and 13th Corps troops at Mersa Metruh nearly led to a botched retreat. At the opening of the first engagement at this location, Claude Auchinleck organized his forces along the Ruweisat Ridge. At the second battle at this location, the British employed Operation Lightfoot as a means of bypassing a minefield. During this battle, British tanks rallied from the namesake railway station to attack the enemy's gasoline supply at Tel el Aqqaqir. Name this location of two WWII battles, the site of Bernard Montgomery's greatest victory over Erwin Rommel.

This ruler was supposedly punished by a deity with famine after suppressing a revolt in Subartu, and he had earlier dealt with an invasion led by four great Elamite generals. He began his reign following the defeat of a King of Umma, Lugulzaggesi, who had fought a war against Ur-Zababa. After taking Kish from Lugulzaggesi, he built his empire by extending trade from his capital city throughout to Susa and the Zagros mountains. He was succeeded by his sons Rimush and Manishtushu, and made his daughter Enheduanna the high priestess of Nanna. Name this former sandal-bearer, a possible inspiration for the biblical Nimrod, a great king of Akkad.

One king of this name and number married Joan of Navarre and fended off the "Epiphany Uprising." Another king by this name and number had Maximilian de Bethune, Duke de Sully negotiate the Peace of Savoy, but was assassinated by Francois Ravalliac. Yet another ruler of this name and number dealt with the rise of anti-king Rudolf of Swabia, and had installed Clement III as pope, though he had earlier traveled to Canossa to reconcile with Pope Gregory VII. Identify this name and number shared by the Holy Roman Emperor involved in the Investiture controversy as well as the Bourbon king of Navarre who declared that "Paris is worth a Mass."

The losing army in this battle was hampered by an inability to rendezvous with Colonel Barry St. Leger's force of mostly Iroquois Indians. The retreating army at this battle paused to bury one of their generals, Simon Fraser, who had been killed the previous day. The losing commander, fresh off a retaking of Fort Ticonderoga, never received aid from Henry Clinton and was defeated when enemy reinforcements under Benedict Arnold arrived. Name this battle which took place in September and October 1777, in which American forces under Horatio Gates defeated John Burgoyne's British forces, fought at Bemis Heights and Freeman's Farm.

One ruler of this country gained power through the revolt of sargents by overthrowing a leader who had organized a secret police called the Porra. This country saw rebellions led by free black men such as Nicholas Morales and Jose Antonio Aponte in 1795 and 1812 respectively. This country also saw Carlos Manuel de Cespedes issue the Grito de Yara which led to the Ten Years War. The United States Congress also declared it did not wish to occupy this country through the Teller Amendment. Identify this country in which Fulgencio Batista was overthrown in 1959 by Fidel Castro.

This man won an important early political victory by contrasting his views against that of his segregationist opponent, George Mahoney, who used the slogan "Your Home is Your Castle--Protect It." Upon election, he alienated liberals by ordering the arrest of protesters at Bowie State College and blaming H. Rap Brown and SNCC for the riots in Cambridge in 1967. His conservatism was further seen in a later position, in which he mocked liberals as "nattering nabobs." This governor of Maryland was selected as a running mate in 1968. Name this vice president who resigned in 1973 over a bribery scandal, the first vice-president of Richard Nixon.

This dynasty adopted a law code called the Yassa and considered "southerners" its lowest class, and it saw the introduction of paper money and Arabic numerals. It finished off its predecessor at the Battle of Yamen and established its capital at Dadu. Problems faced by this dynasty included its costly military campaigns against Java and a successful revolt that saw Zhu Yuanzhang declare himself Hongwu Emperor and found the Ming Dynasty, the Red Turban Rebellion. Name this Chinese dynasty that hosted Marco Polo and attempted to invade Japan, but is best known for being founded by the leader of the Mongols, Kublai Khan.

The youngest man to hold this position defeated machine politician John Hylan in a World War I era election. This first holder of this position after the polity it governs was consolidated created its public transportation system and is Robert Van Wyck. In addition to John Mitchel, the first and only black man to serve in this position was David Dinkins. The holder of this position is entitled to live in a house located in Carl Schurz Park, called Gracie Mansion. A former holder of this position co-sponsored a bill with Norris that outlawed yellow dog contracts. Name this position held by people like Fiorello La Guardia, Rudy Giuliani, and Michael Bloomberg.

This man funded a military corps known as the streltsy, which led to the annexations of Kazan and Astrakhan. At one point during this man's rule, he abdicated the throne and was replaced by Simeon Bekbulatovich. Difficulties in his later years included a botched military campaign to retake western Slavic lands in the Livonian War, and the harsh government he created called the oprichnina, a far cry from his earlier Chosen Council. He killed his own son, bringing about the downfall of the Rurik Dynasty. Identify this Russian leader who served as the first man to take the title tsar and is best known for his rampant acts of cruelty.

During one of this man's military campaigns, he left the government in the hands of Hubert Walter. Earlier, he had become embroiled in a campaign against the Gascons, who had revolted against his rule, while yet another conflict saw him conquering Messina and forcing a treaty that named Tancred the king of Sicily. He died while besieging the castle at Chalus. This victor over the Saracens at Acre was separated from his wife, Berengaria of Navarre, when he was captured by Duke Leopold, who handed him over to his enemy Henry VI. Name this British monarch, who went on the Third Crusade, the brother of John noted for his lion-heartedness.

This document's second article grants one party "undisturbed possession" of its Lands and Estates Forests Fisheries and was preceded by a declaration of independence written by James Busby. One of this agreement's versions was produced by Henry and Edward Williams, and it was preceded by the Musket War. The signing of this document was followed by the killing of 22 British mercenaries in the Wairau Massacre led by Te Rauparaha in an attempt to uphold its continuation of Rangatiratanga, or chieftainship. Co-authored by William Hobson and signed by 500 Maori chiefs, identify this treaty that created the British colony of New Zealand.

One leader of this group reasserted power after Charles of Valois dissolved the government of the Cherchi, and they fought a war against Ezzelino III at the battle of Cassano d'Adda with the help of Ezzelino's brother in law Manfred I. They were massacred in a battle during which they were betrayed by Bocca degli Abati, and they are named for the Bavarian Dukes who opposed the rise of the Hohenstaufens. Dante Alighieri was a member of the white party of this group, which held power in cities such as Genoa and Mantua. Identify this faction that allied with the papacy and opposed the Ghibellines.

He won the presidency after declaring the so-called "war at the top," which pitted him against his former intellectual advisers. As president, he proposed a "NATO bis," a shadow NATO for countries not part of the main organization. His wife, Danuta, claimed his Nobel Peace Prize for him in 1983. Ousted from the presidency by Aleksander Kwasniewski in 1995, this man was previously honored for his work in leading a concerted group action at the shipyards of Gdansk in August of 1980. Identify this man, the president of Poland from 1980 to 1985, who served as the head of the first free trade union within the Soviet bloc, Solidarity.

In this work's supplement, the apocalypse will bring about a new world made of non-living material that beautified by fire and a new heaven and hell. This work's third section discusses the role of the inherent grace of the sacraments in the salvation of the soul, and its second section formulates the doctrines of just war and natural law and is entitled "Ethics." This work's first section contains the author's analysis of the nature of the universe and his Five Proofs of the existence of God. Attempting to apply Aristotelian logic to Catholic theology, identify this scholastic work of theology by Thomas Aquinas.

Two of this man's subordinates ordered the murder by a car bomb in Washington, D.C. Of Orlando Letelie. Less than a decade after taking power, this man pushed forward a new Constitution that declared the armed forces the "guarantors of institutionality." As leader, this man enforced his rule with a security apparatus called the National Intelligence Directorate, and received economic advice students of Milton Friedman dubbed the "Chicago Boys." He was arrested in 1998 in the U.K. On a warrant from the Spanish government. Name this man who replaced Salvador Allende in a 1973 coup, the former dictator of Chile.

The Enham regulations were drawn up by Wulfstan II, who served as an advisor to both this man and his successor. His reign saw Byrhtnoth lose the Battle of Maldon to the Vikings, and this king also paid a gigantic Danegeld to stop the armies of Thorkell the Tall. He was saved from an attacking army by Ulfcytel after ordering the St. Brice's Day massacre and enraging his rival Sweyn Forkbeard. Eventually supplanted as King of England by Sweyn's son Canute, identify this father of Edward the Confessor whose nickname comes from his "ill counsel" rather than his unpreparedness.

This treaty's tenth article calls "traffic in slaves irreconcilable with the principles of humanity and justice," and its ninth article urges the U.S. To end hostilities with the Indians and restore their land. This treaty promised to set up numerous commissions to properly decide various boundary disputes, thus dodging the issues that precipitated the war it ended. The primary American negotiators were two future secretaries of state, Henry Clay and John Quincy Adams. Identify this treaty signed in Belgium on December 24, 1814, before the Battle of New Orleans, but which still marked the official end of the War of 1812.

One king from this country came to power after defeating his mother Teresa at the battle of St. Mamede, and the remnants of Celtic inhabitations in this country are called citanias. H. R. Lang compiled a book of songs written during the reign of King Dennis I of this country, and another of its rulers came to power after defeating John of Castile at the Battle of Aljubarrota. Another king from this country captured the port city of Ceuta. That king established the city of Sagres and was the founder of the Aviz dynasty, and it signed the Treaty of Tordesillas with Spain. Name this country, home of the Braganza dynasty and Henry the Navigator.

Friar Valverde allegedly gave this person a Bible, but this man didn't know how to open a book, and threw it at the Friar's face. This son of Paccha was the highest-ranking casualty in the so-called War of the Two Brothers. His downfall was chronicled by Garcilaso de la Vega, and this man was supposed to be traded for the "ransom room" full of precious metals, but the Europeans reneged and had him strangled instead. After his defeat at Cajamarca, his half-brother Husacar was installed as a puppet ruler. Name this man who was defeated by Francisco Pizarro, the last king of the Incans.

The "Tun" one of these was the site of the first American Masonic Lodge and the first U.S. Marine recruiting drive. One of these structures named "White Horse" was the site of the first Rhode Island state assembly. George Washington's Cincinnatus-like farewell to his troops took place in one of these entities named for Fraunces. The Cantamount one in Bennington was the meeting place of the Green Mountain Boys, and the Battle of Pea Ridge is alternately known as the Battle of the "Elkhorn" one. Name these establishments of early America at which one could buy a brewsky.

This man built himself a full-scale residence city in which each of the four quarters had its own presiding deity. During one battle, this man acted on false information that the opposing army was at Aleppo and walked into a trap of 2,500 enemy chariots. He ordered the construction of hypostyle hall at Karnak and statues of himself at Abu Simbel. He conquered Katna and Tunip, revenging his earlier strategic defeat by Muwatilli II that led to the first recorded peace treaty, with Hattusili I. Name this Egyptian pharaoh who succeeded Seti I and fought the Hittites at Kadesh, who reigned during such prosperity that he received the epithet "the Great."

This religion teaches that God has made three offers of amnesty to man, the third of which was the most perfect and the only one to not require a prophet. Places of worship in this religion are often decorated with spheres and it was once common for members of this religion to attempt to communicate with their dead ancestors, sometimes using ouija boards. The major symbol of this religion is the left eye of God, which decorates its altars and buildings. This religion's name means "High Tower" and its ecclesiastical structure mimics that of the Catholic Church with bishops and a pope. Most notable for making saints out of Sun Yat Sen and Victor Hugo, for ten points name this syncretic 20th century religion from Vietnam.

King Atta-hushu of these peoples introduced worship of the goddess Anunitum among them, but she was abandoned after his death. A shrine to the goddess Upurkuppak can be found at these peoples' temple complex of Chogha Zanbil, and in the north of their lands the goddess Pinikir was venerated. They worshipped the earth god Humban and the major triad of their pantheon was led by Inshushinak. The fact that they had a major goddess named Kiririsha supports theories that these people were related to the Dravidians. With capital at Susa, for ten points name this ethnic group that in ancient times lived just southeast of Mesopotamia.

This concept was prominently opposed by the Scottish thinker William Welwod, who relied on the authority of Scripture to argue that a well-known theoretical defense of this concept was merely a front for another country's attack on Scottish industry. In the 18th century, the Dutch thinker Cornelius van Bynkershoek introduced the so-called "cannon shot rule," which helped to define this concept. Another Dutch thinker, Dirk Graswinckel, critiqued the views on this concept which were set forth in a 1635 book which marked the first use of Arabic type in England. While John Selden's contributions to the understanding of this concept are justly renowned, you may be more familiar with a book on this concept that opposed a certain Portuguese policy and defended the "Right Which Belongs to the Dutch to Take Part in the East Indian Trade." That work, which takes its title from this concept, is by Hugo Grotius. Name this right of every nation to make commerce upon the waves.

Monasteries in this country include the Celie Monastery. Despite not being named Simeon, one ruler from this country was canonized as "St. Simeon the Myrrh-Flowing", while the Orthodox church in this country owns the finger of St. Paraskevi. A 20th century bishop from this country was nicknamed "The New Chrysostom" for his oratory and died in exile in Libertyville, IL. Apart from Nikolai Velmirovich, another notable saint from this country was a prince of the Nemanjic dynasty named Sava. In recent times, this Cyrillic-using country has targeted Muslim ethic Albanians for ethnic cleansing. Name this Balkan country with capital at Belgrade.

Prior to this church council, the heresy that this council dealt with was criticized by Eusebius of Dorylaeum, and this church council condemned the views of Patriarch John of Antioch. The heresy condemned at this coun cil was strongly criticized by Eutyches, who would later be condemned for leading the Monophysite heresy. This council's target heresy held that the two natures of Jesus were separate and opposed using the word "theotokos" to describe Mary. However, the heresy condemned here was subsequently adopted by the Assyrian Church of the East and became popular with Central Asian Christians. Name this 431 church council that condemned Nestorianism.

This man became involved in a public debate about "vitiation" after he recently co-authored a book with Bryan Garner. This man argued that religious belief strengthens moral justification for capital punishment in his 2002 essay "God's Law and Ours". This man argues for an expansive view of the confrontation clause, such as by requiring that DNA evidence can be challenged. He outlined his views in A Matter of Interpretation, where he argued that recognizing a word's unchanging definition is the "lesser evil" when compared to the living document approach, and in the majority opinion in District of Columbia v. Heller he stated that the Second Amendment included a personal right to own a firearm. Name this conservative legal theorist associated with "original meaning", the first Italian-American appointed to the Supreme Court.

A biography of this man was written by the historian Philostorgius, a member of a sect that claimed to follow this man, the Anomoeans. This man's followers during his life included Secundus and Theonus. Marcellus of Ancyra wrote a condemnation of this man that was later condemned as heretical. This student of St. Lucian of Antioch first became notable as an opponent of Alexander of Alexandria. This theologian accused his opponents of the Sabellian heresy. To make theology accessible to the public, he put his views into poetry in his most famous work, Thalia. Name this Egyptian heretic condemned at the Council of Nicea, who taught that Jesus was created by God.

In this nation, Calixto Garcia and others who refused to accept the Pact of Zanjon fought a continuation of another conflict known as the Little War. Generals who accepted the aforementioned peace included Maximo Gomez and Antonio Maceo, who supported a man whose Grito de Yara began the Ten Years War, Carlos Manuel de Cespedes. The final war for independence in this nation saw the atrocities of Butcher Weyler, and in 1895, the death of its early leader Jose Marti. Name this Caribbean nation which gained its independence from Spain after a war which the United States began after the sinking of the USS Maine in its port of Havana.

Upon coronation, this ruler had his father's ministers Edmund Dudley and Richard Empson, who had been involved in the Council Learned in the Law, convicted of treason and executed. Historian Edward Hall, a contemporary of this ruler, wrote about how this man had Henry Courtenay executed for his leading role in the Exeter Conspiracy, which may not have existed. This ruler defeated troops under Jacques de la Palice with the help of Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian I at the Battle of the Spurs. Robert Aske led the Pilgrimage of Grace in opposition to the rule of this man and the Dissolution of the Monasteries, which had been enacted by this ruler after the passage of the Acts of Supremacy, which gave him control over his country's churches. Served by ministers such as Wolsey and Cranmer, name this leader of the Protestant Reformation in England, a Tudor monarch who had six wives.

Ambassador Otto Magnus von Stackelberg threatened the destruction of a city if the first of these was not accepted, and Lowenwolde's Treaty, also known as the Treaty of the Three Black Eagles, was a precursor to them. A legislative meeting which bears the name of Nicholas Repnin provoked the War of the Confederation of Bar, which precipitated the first of these. The War in Defense of the Constitution, fought between reformers and the Targowica Confederation, resulted in the second of these, which was accepted by the Grodno Sejm [same]. Count Kaunitz pushed the first of these through against the will of Maria Theresa, and the third of these was sparked by the rebellion of Tadeusz Kosciuszko. Name these three treaties in which Austria, Prussia and Russia divided up an Eastern European nation with capital at Warsaw.

The Silhak movement began in this empire as a reaction to the Sarim, also called "forest of scholars", who rigidly upheld Neo-Confucian ideals. During its waning years, this empire faced the Gapsin Coup and Imo Mutiny, and Pierre-Gustave Roze led an unsuccessful invasion of this in 1866. The Gabo Reform in this empire had the intention of ending the Donghak Peasant Revolution, and in the Imjin War, this empire used turtle ships to fight off two Japanese invasions led by Toyotomi Hideyoshi. This empire's only ruler known as the great, Sejong, created an alphabet known as the Hangul, and its ruling House of Yi was established by its founder, Taejo. Ended by the Treaty of Shimonoseki following the First Sino-Japanese War, name this successor of the Goryeo Dynasty which ruled Korea for over five hundred years.

The weakness of the army after this event provoked an uprising led by a man who promised that his enemy's bullets would change to water and their cannon shells would become eggs, Mlimo. Graham John Bower wrote the Secret History of this event, which was a reaction to the closing of all river fords known as the Drifts Crisis. Governor-General Hercules Robinson was contacted by Joseph Chamberlain during this event because the latter feared that the timing of it would ruin him as Colonial Secretary. This invasion began at Pitsani, but only four days later the attackers surrendered at Doornkoop to Piet Cronje. This invasion hinged on an uprising by ill-treated expatriate workers known as Uitlanders which never happened, and in response to this Kaiser Wilhelm II sent a congratulatory telegram to Paul Kruger. Name this 1895 British raid on Transvaal which helped start the Second Boer War in South Africa.

After the death of fur trapper Ewing Young, this region was left without a government until the Champoeg Meetings created the Organic Laws, which set up a provisional government. John McLoughlin is seen as the father of this region, and the Whitman Massacre here sparked the Cayuse War. Henry James Warre and Mervin Vavasour were sent to scout this region in case a war broke out over it, but it never came to that, although Lyman Cutler's shooting of an animal did spark the bloodless Pig War here. Missouri Senator Lewis Linn was a champion of annexing this region, and a dispute over the boundary of this region led to the slogan "Fifty-four Forty or Fight!" but James Polk settled for the 49th parallel as its northern border in an 1846 treaty with Great Britain. Name this region of the Pacific Northwest, the namesake of a trail used by pioneers.

After conquest by Quintus Caecilius Metellus, Gortyn served as the Roman capital of this, and it is home to one of the last refuges of the kri-kri, which is found at its Samaria Gorge. After the Fourth Crusade, this island came under the rule of Venetians, who called their capital Candia, and its mountain ranges include the Dedros and Dikti. This island's Amari Valley was the center of the resistance movement during German occupation following Operation Mercury, and its highest point is Mount Ida, where Zeus was supposedly born. With capital at Heraklion, name this largest Greek island on which the Minoan site of Knossos lies.

This ruler's physician Moses Hamon got him to denounce blood libels against Jews, and he had his concubine Mahidevran or Gulbahar banished for beating his wife. This ruler died of natural causes during the Siege of Szigetvar, at which a tiny Croatian force under Nikola Zrinski delayed his army of 100,000 for over a month. This ruler's Code of the Rayas lifted many of his subjects from serfdom, and together with his Grand Mufti Ebussuud he brought Qanun closer to Sharia. At the Battle of Preveza, Hayreddin Barbarossa won a victory which secured this man's domination of the eastern Mediterranean, and he appointed John Zapolya King of Hungary after the death of Louis II at the Battle of Mohacs. The husband of Roxelana, name this son of Selim the Grim, an Ottoman Sultan of the sixteenth century known as "the magnificent".

Divisions and seize bridges at Grave, Eindhoven and Nijmegen. This operation was the last Allied attempt to win the war by Christmas, and it failed to secure a crossing point of the Rhine at Arnhem. Name this failed 1944 offensive through the Netherlands, the largest airborne operation in history.

A forty-eight parchment manuscript full of descriptions of the banners left on the field of this battle is called the Banderia Prutenorum and was written by Johannes Longinus. Prior to this battle, the Peace of Raciaz was signed to put an end to the first Samogitian Urpsing, although the second one led directly to this engagement. The conflict in which this battle took place was ended by the Peace of Thorn, and victory here was made possible by the Union of Krewo. The victorious side in this battle placed the Drewenz River at their backs, and this battle was fought between the towns of Stebark and Ludwigsdorf. In this engagement, Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen was defeated by the combined forces of Vytautas the Great and Wladyslaw II Jagiello. Name this 1410 victory for Poland-Lithuania over the Teutonic Knights.

In this conflict, a man known as the "Red Prince", General Lynch, led a raid of Chinese immigrants north to collect debt, and during it the United States attempted to broker a peace deal on board the Lackawanna. The first engagement of this conflict was a defense of two destroyed bridges near the town of Calama known as the Battle of Topater. During this war, President Mariano Prado left for Europe and was overthrown by Nicolas de Pierola. The naval theatre of this war centered on the Huascar, which sank the Esmeralda at the Battle of Iquique but was captured during the Battle of Angamos. This conflict was caused by the breakdown of negotiations between Hilarion Daza and Anibal Pinto, and it resulted in the exchange of Arica and Tacna through the Treaty of Ancon in 1883. Name this conflict between Bolivia, Peru and Chile over the nitrate-rich Atacama Desert which is named for a nearby body of water.

The Battle of Annaberg was the largest engagement of this region's namesake uprisings, and this region's economy was based on coal mining in its Rybnik area. This region was the site of the 1241 Battle of Liegnitz in which its ruler Henry II the Pious was killed by Mongols. The peace agreement which ended the War of the Bavarian Succession was signed in this region's city of Teschen. The cities of Ostrava and Troppau are the largest in the small portion of this region which lies in one country, and its city of Opole served as the capital of its Upper section. The Oder River begins in this region, and Katowice and Wroclaw are its largest cities. This region borders Moravia and Saxony, and it was captured by Prussia in the War of the Austrian Succession. Name this Polish region on the border of the Czech Republic and Germany.

This state made an alliance with the Kingdom of Jerusalem through the Pactum Warmundi, and the oldest history of it is provided by John the Deacon. This entity's dissolution was confirmed in the Peace of Leoben, and it had earlier defeated one of its rivals in the War of Chioggia. Pope Julius II initially organized the League of Cambrai to combat the power of this state, although it later fought alongside the papacy in the Battle of Lepanto. This polity's blind leader Enrico Dandolo had his rivals attacked in the Siege of Zara, and also diverted the Fourth Crusade in an attack on Constantinople. Ruled by a Doge, name this rival of Genoa, a maritime power in northeastern Italy on the Adriatic Sea.

This incident resulted in the creation of a movement against similar activities by Eliphalet Nott and Lyman Beecher. Both William Van Ness and David Hosack provide firsthand accounts of this, and one of the participants had already engaged in similar activities with William Gordon, Aedanus Burke and John Mercer. This event was carried out with supplies of John Baker Church and it resulted in one participant being carried to the home of William Bayard. Causes of this event include animosity over one man's father-in-law, Philip Schuyler, losing a Senate seat and that same man's support of Morgan Lewis as Governor of New York. Identify this occurrence in Weehawken, New Jersey in 1804 between the sitting Vice President and the former first Secretary of the Treasury.

During tsar Alexei's reign, an uprising occurred in Moscow over Boris Morozov's imposition of a tax on this commodity, and the French gabelle was also an unpopular tax on it. The towns which produced this commodity in England were appended with the suffix "wich" and were concentrated in Cheshire and Worcestershire. The Azalai is a route for caravans that carried this commodity across the Sahara, after which it was traded for gold, and the origins of the Hanseatic League lie in the trading of this commodity, which was used to preserve fish. Name this commodity, the subject of British taxation which sparked a march by Gandhi.

This entity negotiated the Treaty of Dumplin Creek with Alexander Outlaw, which set its southern border as the Little River. Governor Esteban Miro sent gold to entice this entity, and James White attempted to place it under Spanish rule. This entity's first proposed constitution prohibited doctors, lawyers and priests from election to its legislature, and the economic system of this entity was bartering. William Cocke defended this entity from a force sent by Governor Richard Caswell, and John Tipton defeated the militia of its Governor John Sevier. Native American raids finally ended this entity, and it then returned to North Carolina, although it later became part of Tennessee. Name this attempted US state named for a Founding Father from Pennsylvania.

On the last day of this engagement, reinforcements under Sedullos and Vercassivellaunos arrived, and the focuse of this battle was the capital of the Mandubii. Prior to this battle, Ambiorix led the Eburones in revolt, which resulted in a meeting at Bibracte that elected a ruler of the Arverni to lead a new rebellion. During this battle, Commius arrived with reinforcements that unsuccessfully attacked the Romans, who were fortified between a contravallation wall and the namesake city. Fought shortly after the Battle of Gergovia, name this 52 BC victory for Julius Caesar over Vercingetorix, which resulted in Roman control over Gaul.

William Edgett Smith wrote a biography of this man titled We Must Run While They Walk. This man was opposed by his advisor Oscar Kambona on some of his policies, and he formed Chama Cha Mapinduzi, also known as the Party of the Revolution, which he continued to lead for five years after stepping down as president. This man appointed Ali Hassan Mwinyi as his successor, and he later backed Benjamin Mkapa as president over Jakaya Kikwete. This man was instrumental in the coup which brought France-Albert Rene to power in Seychelles, and also in installing Yusuf Lule as president of a bordering nation. The concept of ujamaa formed the basis of this man's socialist ideas, which were laid out in the Arusha Declaration, and his forces toppled the regime of Idi Amin in Uganda. Name this African leader, the first President of Tanzania.

This faction had men such as Thomas Usk, Simon Burley and Nicholas Brembre executed. The impeachment of Michael de la Pole in the so-called Wonderful Parliament led to the ascension of this group, and their victory at the Battle of Radcot Bridge over Robert de Vere resulted in unlimited power for them. This group was led by Thomas of Woodstock, the first Duke of Gloucester, and in the Merciless Parliament, this faction purged the entire royal court and made the king a puppet. The power of this group waned with the return of John of Gaunt to England, and unfortunately for the reigning king, he made the generous decision to not punish the future Henry IV for his participation in this group. Name this group of barons which held almost unrestricted power in England from 1387 to 1389, during the reign of Richard II.

This ruler was chosen to succeed Uttama after the assassination of Aditya II, and it is believed that the city of Nagapatnam served as his chief naval base. This ruler made Polonnaruwa the capital of one region after he captured its King Mahinda V and destroyed its capital of Anuradhapura. After success in the Kandalur War, this ruler took a name which means "the king who wears three crowns", and he was able to extend his empire's borders to the Tungabhadra River by fighting King Satyasraya of the Chalukyas. This ruler had the Brihadeeswarar Temple built in his capital of Tanjore on his return from a campaign that began the conquest of Sri Lanka, a goal which was completed by his son Rajendra. Name this Tamil leader who established the Chola Empire in the tenth century.

Following the February Uprising, this ruler declared the Social Democratic Party illegal and made the Vaterlandische Front or Fatherland's Front the only party. Emil Fey and Ernst Starhemberg, the leaders of the paramilitary group Heimwehr, served as Vice Chancellors of this man. This politician formed an alliance with Hungarian Prime Minister Gyula Gombos, and at a meeting in Riccione, the independence of this man's country was guaranteed by Mussolini. Theodor Habicht organized the coup against this man known as the July Putsch, although it was Otto Planetta who assassinated him. Succeeded as Chancellor by Kurt Schuschnigg, name this Austrian Fascist dictator who resisted the Anschluss with Germany.

In cases where this policy was lacking or nonexistent, the practice of taqiyya was often used for protection by concealing one's identity. Although this principle was advocated by Pope Alexander II, he sanctioned the War of Barbastro which ended in a massacre that defied it. This principle was upheld in the sixty-seven articles of the Capitulation of Granada regarding Moriscos, which was signed by Boabdil, but it was largely ignored after Cardinal Talavera's replacement by Cardinal Cisneros. Tomas de Torquemada was one of the chief opponents of this principle, and the Alhambra Decree was another step back in achieving this policy, because through it, Ferdinand and Isabella expelled Jews from their country. Name this policy which was severely lacking in Iberia during the Spanish Inquisition.

Baha ad-Din wrote the Rare and Excellent History of this ruler, who rose to prominence following a power struggle between Amalric I, Shawar and Shirkuh. This ruler took the lands of As-Salih Ismail after the death of the Zengid ruler Nur ad-Din, and he twice failed to take Krak des Chevaliers. A small force under King Baldwin IV managed to kill ninety percent of this man's army at the Battle of Montgisard, and he signed the Treaty of Ramla which gave his enemies a strip of land from Jaffa to Tyre. Following the Siege of Tiberias, this ruler defeated the exhausted, thirsty forces of Raymond III of Tripoli and captured Guy of Lusignan at the Battle of Hattin. This ruler abolished the Ismaili Fatimid Caliphate and founded the Ayyubid Dynasty in its place. Name this opponent of Richard the Lionheart whose 1187 capture of Jerusalem sparked the Third Crusade.

William Charles' LEAP NO LEAP cartoon attacked this meeting, and Letters Developing the Character and Views of this as well as Letters in Defense of this were written by the man who served as its leader. During this meeting Caleb Strong, the Governor of Massachusetts, went on a secret peace mission which attempted to trade northern Maine to Great Britain, and its unofficial leader was Harrison Gray Otis. The amendments proposed at this meeting included a limitation of Congress' embargo power to sixty days, an end of the Three-fifths compromise and one which would have prevented presidents from being elected from the same state for more than two successive terms. This meeting was attended by members of the Essex Junto, who supported secession, and it was a reaction to the Non-Intercourse Act and Embargo Act of 1807. Resulting in the demise of the Federalist Party, name this meeting of New England states during the War of 1812 which was rendered ineffectual by the signing of the Treaty of Ghent.

This ruler made Milo the Archbishop of Rheims, and with this man's blessing, Willibrord, known as the Apostle to the Frisians, built the Abbey of Echternach. King Redbad, the last independent ruler of the Frisians, delivered this man his only defeat at the Battle of Cologne, although this man would later revenge his loss. This man defeated Ragenfrid and Chilperic II at the battles of Ambleve and Vincy, after which they allied with Odo the Great of Aquitaine, only to be defeated by this man at the Battle of Soissons. The son of the concubine Alpaida and Pepin of Herstal, this man is best remembered for his victory over Abdul Rahman Al Ghafiqi, an Umayyad general, which halted Muslim conquest of Europe. Name this Frankish ruler who won the Battle of Tours.

This politician agreed to receive aid from the United States in exchange for use of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec via the McLane-Ocampo Treaty, but it was never ratified by the Senate. As Minister of Justice in the government of Juan Alvarez this man enacted his namesake law which abolished special privileges for the clergy and military, and he served as Vice President under Ignacio Comonfort. This man was arrested by supporters of the Plan of Tacubaya, which put his rival Felix Zuloaga in power, but he escaped and defeated Zuloaga in the Reform War. This politician's cancellation of all foreign debt resulted in the occupation of Vera Cruz by Spain, Great Britain and France, but his forces soon won the Battle of Puebla. Earlier in his career, this man had helped draft the Plan of Ayutla, which ousted Santa Anna. Name this Zapotec from Oaxaca, Mexico's revered liberal president who drove out the French forces of Emperor Maximilian.

This country contains the ancient footprints of Acahualinca, which were made in volcanic ash, and its Bosawas Biosphere Reserve protects the Western Hemisphere's second largest rainforest. Diriangen led the Chorotegas of this country in their resistance to the Conquistador Gil Gonzalez Davila, and its old capital was destroyed by an eruption of Momotombo. The largest port on the east coast of this country is named after a Dutch pirate, Abraham Blauvelt, and once served as the capital of its Mosquito Coast. This nation leased its Corn Islands to the United States in the Bryan-Chamorro Treaty in 1914, and its former capital of Granada served as the seat of government for the filibuster William Walker. Bordered by Costa Rica and Honduras, name this Central American nation with capital at Managua.

This politician signed an agreement with Francisco Peynado which ended American occupation of the Dominican Republic, and as an Associate Justice, he wrote the majority opinion in Bailey v. Alabama which found peonage laws to be unconstitutional. This man attempted to curb the growing power of Japan through the Washington Naval Conference, which he chaired as Secretary of State under Coolidge, and he defeated William Randolph Hearst to become Governor of New York. This politician penned the majority opinion in the Sick Chicken Case, and he led the opposition to Roosevelt's court-packing scheme. This man's presidential ticket with Charles Fairbanks fell 4,000 votes short in California to a man whose campaign slogan was "He kept us out of war", and Herbert Hoover appointed him to the position he is most notable for to replace William Howard Taft. Name this loser of the 1916 presidential election to Woodrow Wilson who served as Chief Justice from 1930 to 1941.

The failure of the Convention of Pardo led to this conflict, and during it, George Anson led a fleet of eight ships which circumnavigated the globe and attacked enemy shipping along the way. One battle in this conflict saw four thousand soldiers and six ships under the command of Blas de Lezo defeat an invasion force of almost two hundred ships commanded by Admiral Vernon, the disastrous Battle of Cartagena de Indias. The early stages of this war are highlighted by the capture of the Panamanian city of Porto Bello, and at the Battle of Bloody Marsh during it, James Oglethorpe defended Georgia from an attack which originated in Florida. This conflict was fought over the Asiento, a contract dealing with the control of the slave trade, and it led to the fall of Robert Walpole's government. Name this early phase of the War of the Austrian Succession, a conflict between England and Spain named after a certain British captain's severed appendage.

This figure designates the numeral one or Oan as the divine, which is typographically depicted by an arc flying off. In one of this man's hymns, he claims that "Only the relisher of fragrance can recognize the flower." In another hymn, the Japu, he articulates the notion of Ik Oankar and suggests that humans must be committed to removing dualites or dubida. During this figure's lifetime Ibrahim Lodi was defeated at the Battle of Panipat, leading this figure to compose the Baburvani, which criticizes the narrow worldview of Babur's Mughal Empire. Recorded by Bhai Gurdas, the janamsakhis are the collected mythologies of this figure's birth. At his death it is said that his body disappeared and flowers remained so that he could be cremated or buried and after his vision at Sultanpur, he proclaimed, "There is no Hindu; there is no Muslim." name this first of the ten Sikh Gurus.

The beginning of this event was heralded in a speech on the twentieth anniversary of Victorious February which claimed that Klement Gottwald had failed in his handling of the trial of Rudolf Slansky. Ota Sik's "third way" was the underlying economic policy of this period, and a meeting at Cierna nad Tisou failed to put an end to it. The weakness of the Action Programme during this period led Ludvik Vaculik to publish a document which called for the resignation of inept leaders, the "Two Thousand Words". This event began after the resignation of Antonin Novotny, and in response to the end of it, Jan Palach set himself on fire in protest. Gustav Husak became President after this event was crushed by a Warsaw Pact invasion, which was justified by the Brezhnev Doctrine. This period was led by Alexander Dubcek, who attempted to create "socialism with a human face". Name this period of liberal reforms in Czechoslovakia in 1968.

While securing the junction of this battle's namesake feature and Portage Road, forces under Thomas Jesup captured William Hamilton Merritt. This engagement was the subject of historian Donald Grave's book Where Right and Glory Lead! James Miller is regarded as the hero of this battle for capturing the enemy's artillery during it, and this battle was fought a few weeks after the American victory at the Battle of Chippewa. At this battle, the Glengarry Light Infantry were forced to withdraw by friendly fire during Gordon Drummond's counterattack, and prior to this, Commodore Isaac Chauncey was unable to get reinforcements to the army which wanted to attack Fort George. A bloody, indecisive battle that resulted in an American retreat to Fort Erie, this battle saw the capture of Phineas Riall as well as the wounding of both American commanders, Jacob Brown and Winfield Scott. Name this 1814 battle fought near Niagara Falls during the US invasion of Canada in the War of 1812.

Although this ruler's servant Jauhar wrote a biography of him, the most notable account of his life is provided by his sister, Gulbadan Begum. This man's defeat at the battles of Chausa and Kannauj resulted in his flight from India, and during his exile he converted to Shia Islam in exchange for military aid from Shah Tahmasp. With that aid, this man was able to take Kabul from his disloyal half-brother Kamran Mirza, and he defeated the successors of Sher Shah Suri and retook Delhi after appointing Bairam Khan to lead his army. This man is noted for the tomb built for him by his wife Hamida, and after his return from exile he succeeded in reunifying the empire of his father Babur. Name this ruler, the second Mughal Emperor and father of Akbar.

With the help of Archbishop Simon Atumano, Juan de Urtubia was able to wrest control of this city from the Catalan Company in the fourteenth century. While in an alliance with Argos, this city lost the Battle of Coronea to Agesilaus II, although at the start of that conflict this city defeated Sparta at the Battle of Haliartus and killed Lysander. This city won a pyrrhic victory at the Battle of Mantinea, at which three of its generals died, one of whom had earlier pioneered the use of the oblique order tactic in the Battle of Leuctra. At the Battle of Chaeronea, this city's Sacred Band was finally defeated at the hands of Phillip II and Alexander the Great. Name this city in Boetia, the most powerful Greek city-state prior to the death of its general Epaminondas and the subsequent conquest by Macedonia.

Romano Bonaventura summoned the Council of Bourges to fund this military venture and Peter Vaux de Cernay is the principle primary source for it. Peter II of Aragon fought in this conflict until his death at the Battle of Muret, and it began after the murder of Pierre de Castelnau. Arnaud Amalric, the abbot of Citeaux, was responsible for much of the recruitment for this venture and when asked how to distinguish friends from enemies he reportedly said, "Kill them all, for the Lord knows them that are His." In this conflict, Raymond VI of Toulouse regained much of his territories after the death of Simon de Montford and the failure of Louis VIII's campaigns. This military venture began after Saint Dominic's failed attempted at converting heretics in the Languedoc region, and it contributed to the start of the Inquisition. Name this crusade called by Pope Innocent III against Cathars in southern France.

This nation signed the Armistice of Focsani after its disastrous entry into World War One following the success of the Brusilov Offensive, and later, this country was the subject of Operation Tidal Wave, an unsuccessful American bombing raid which sought to incapacitate its Ploesti oil fields that were driving the Nazi war machine. Prior to World War Two, this country was ruled by the fascist Iron Guard, but after the Legionnaires' Rebellion that party was outlawed by Ion Antonescu. After the abdication of King Michael, this country was ruled by Gheorghe Gheorghiu-Dej and later the author of the July Theses who was executed with his wife Elena in 1989. Name this Eastern European country which was ruled by the communist Nicolae Ceausescu and has its capital at Bucharest.

One member of this party, Levi Boone, incited the Lager Beer Riot when he proposed closing taverns on Sundays as Mayor of Chicago. John Neely Johnson defeated incumbent John Bigler to become Governor of California on this ticket, and Nathaniel Banks was this party's only Speaker of the House. This party's only national convention was held in Philadelphia, and they chose Andrew Jackson Donelson as their VP candidate. This party was originally founded as the Order of the Star Spangled Banner, and it disintegrated following an election in which it won only Maryland. Members of this party joined former Whigs to form the Constitutional Union Party which nominated Edward Everett and John Bell in the 1860 election, and this party gained its nickname from Horace Greeley. Name this third party which ignored the slavery issue and garnered a fifth of the vote in 1856 for Milliard Fillmore by capitalizing on anti-immigrant and anti-Catholic hysteria.

This politician gained prominence for defending Nils von Schoultz and other Hunter Patriots who participated in the Battle of the Windmill. This man's first government collapsed when a telegram sent to Hugh Allan that mentioned bribery was stolen from John Abbot's office. This politician formed the Great Coalition with George Carter's Parti Bleu and George's Brown's Clear Grits faction, and his National Policy favored high tariffs. This politician purchased Rupert's Land, which became part of the newly formed Northwest Territories, and his administration passed the Manitoba Act in the aftermath of Louis Riel's Red River Rebellion. This man led his country's delegation at the Charlottetown Conference, and his resignation during the Pacific Scandal led to the government of Alexander Mackenzie. Name this first Prime Minister of Canada.

The last section of this work notes that geniuses of legislation are rare and that none has seen fit to utilize the light of the New Testament in 1800 years. The last paragraph of this work asserts that the progress from limited monarchy to true democracy is also the process of greater respect for the individual. This essay attacks a speech by Daniel Webster to the Senate in stating that slavery should remain on the basis of being part of the original constitution. The first section of this essay claims that the American government is nothing more than a tradition that attempts to pass itself down and that none can be associated with it without feeling shame. Beginning with the acceptance of the maxim that "That government governs best which governs least," name this essay by Henry David Thoreau that inspired people like Martin Luther King Jr. And Mohandas Gandhi.

One tactic used by the leader of this rebellion was to have priests bring out salt and water while ringing church bells to signify his arrival. Alexander Bibikov was sent to suppress this rebellion and won a victory at Tatischevo before succumbing to cholera. This rebellion's highpoint was short-lived because Johann Michelson arrived to retake Kazan a day after its capture, and this insurrection was recounted by Pushkin in The Captain's Daughter. The leader of this rebellion was betrayed and sent off in an iron cage to Moscow to be executed after his defeat at Tsaritsyn by Alexander Suvorov. This rebellion incorporated Bashkirs, Old Believers, Yaik Cossacks and Ural mine workers, and its leader proclaimed an end to serfdom. Name this peasant rebellion led by a man who proclaimed himself czar Peter III which challenged the reign of Catherine the Great.

This event began two weeks after the successful Operation Frequent Wind. During this event, Rowland Purser made a dash across the "sunken beach", and flight mechanic John Harston led men to safety after a helicopter crash. A firsthand account of this event is provided by captain Charles Miller. The Coral Sea was dispatched during this event, and like U-Tapao, it served as an air base for the rescuing force. During this event, the Henry Wilson was instrumental in providing covering fire for troops which landed on a beach, and the Harold Holt performed a ship-to-ship boarding which revealed that the hostages had already been evacuated. The main action of this event was an invasion of Koh Tang, which was fruitless because the hostages were being released simultaneously at Kampong Som. Name this 1975 incident involving Cambodian seizure of an American merchant ship, considered the last action of the Vietnam War.

This agreement was negotiated by Luis Mendez de Haro and Hugues de Lionne, one of the architects of the League of the Rhine which prompted it. For its participation in the Reapers' War, one country was awarded Roussillon and Artois in this agreement, and that country also received parts of Flanders and Luxembourg. The English, led by William Lockhart, succeeded in gaining Dunkirk in this agreement, a city which they had captured at the Battle of the Dunes in which Louis II de Bourbon, the Prince of Conde was defeated by the Vicomte de Turenne. In this agreement, the infanta Maria Theresa, daughter of King Philip IV, renounced her claim to the throne in exchange for marrying Louis XIV, but the failure to pay the dowry led to the War of Devolution. Cardinal Mazarin negotiated this treaty, which ended a war between two countries that the Peace of Westphalia had failed to end. Name this 1659 treaty between France and Spain, named for the mountain range which forms their border.

This empire used a system of local government in which an obirempon or "Big Man" served as a regional ruler, and it employed a communication system called "talking drums". This kingdom rose to prominence with its victory over Ntim Gyakari at the Battle of Feyiase, which cemented their dominance over the Denkyira people. This empire's last resistance was led by Queen Yaa in 1900, and their capital had earlier been burned by the British general Garnet Wolseley. This empire's cofounders were Osei Kofi Tutu, who wielded political power, and his chief priest Okomfo Anokye, who made the Golden Stool descend from the heavens. With its capital at Kumasi, name this African empire centered in present-day Ghana.

This man defeated Hal Suit to become governor, and his participation in a primary four years earlier had led to a runoff between Ellis Arnall and Lester Maddox. This man was advised by one subordinate to begin Operation Cyclone, and during his administration, Operation Credible Sport was proposed to correct the disastrous Operation Eagle Claw. This man's Malaise Speech commented on a crisis of confidence among Americans, and in another speech which this man called a fireside chat, he wore a sweater and compared the energy crisis to the "moral equivalent of war". This man threatened to use military force to defend US interests in the Persian Gulf in his namesake doctrine, and with Leonid Brezhnev he signed SALT II. This man signed two treaties with Omar Torrijos which transferred US control over the Panama Canal, and he oversaw the Camp David Accords. Name this former Governor of Georgia whose awful handling of the Iran hostage crisis led to his defeat by Ronald Reagan in the 1980 presidential election.

The campaign leading up to this engagement began following the failure to renew the twenty year old Peace of Vasvar, which had been signed after the Battle of Saint Gotthard. This battle was preceded by a slaughter at Perchtoldsdorf, and it was fought on Kahlenberg Heights. This engagement was preceded by a kuruc uprising led by the Calvinist Imry Thokoly, and Ernst Rudiger von Starhemberg was the commander of the garrison which was besieged prior to it. The decisive action in this battle was history's largest cavalry charge, which was led by 3,000 hussars, and Charles, Duke of Lorraine led the forces of his brother-in-law Leopold I at this battle. Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa was executed for his failure in this battle by Sultan Mehmed IV, and the Christian force was victorious in it due to the aid of John III Sobieski of Poland. Name this 1683 battle which ended Ottoman domination of Eastern Europe outside the capital of the Hapsburg Empire.
